sections.html:
Barbour County sits on the Allegheny Plateau in north-central West Virginia. Philippi is the seat, and the land around it is rugged, drained by the Buckhannon, Middle Fork and Tygart Valley rivers. The county covers 342.9 square miles. U.S. 119 and U.S. 250 cross it north to south, and U.S. 33 clips the southern tip.

The 2020 population was 15,461, with an estimate of 15,414 for 2025. Philippi had 2,928 residents in 2020 and Belington, the next-largest town, had 1,804. Median home value is $106,600, 75.0% of homes are owner-occupied, and median household income is $42,260.

Philippi lies mostly on low ground beside the Tygart Valley River, and water has reached it repeatedly. The worst event was the November 1985 flood. The town has since put a floodplain management plan in place.

Own a house on the river bottom? Before listing, work through this short list:

  • Ask your insurer or title company if the parcel is in a mapped flood zone.
  • Collect invoices for repairs after any earlier water damage.
  • Be ready to tell each buyer about past water in the basement or crawl space.
  • Learn whether a buyer's lender will insist on flood insurance.

A financed sale in a flood-prone spot moves slowly because the lender and insurer both have to approve. Cash buyers skip the lender, though a careful one still looks at the risk.

sections.h2: How the state classifies and assesses property
sections.html:
Nearly all real and tangible personal property in West Virginia is taxable. On July 1 each year the ownership, use and value of a parcel are locked in for the next calendar tax year. Your county assessor puts the value on it; the county sheriff then bills and collects.

Under the state constitution every parcel lands in one of four classes:

  • Class I covers intangible personal property and some farm personal property, and nothing in it is taxed at present.
  • Class II is the owner-occupied house used only as a home, plus farmland worked by its owner or a bona fide tenant.
  • Class III is property outside a municipality that does not fit Class I or II.
  • Class IV is the same kind of property inside a municipality.

Your house is Class II while you live in it. If the buyer rents it out or leaves it empty, it moves to Class III or IV, depending on whether it stands inside a municipality, and the bill can change. Four kinds of body levy the tax: county boards of education, county commissions, municipalities and the State.

DateWhat happens
July 1Ownership, use and value fixed for the next tax year
On or after July 15Tax tickets issued by the sheriff
September 1First installment due, discount ends
October 1First half delinquent, interest begins
December 1Last day for owners 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, to apply for the homestead exemption
February 1 to February 28County commission sits as the board of equalization and review
March 1Second installment due, discount ends
April 1Second half delinquent

To protest a value, appear before the county commission while it sits as the board of equalization and review. The board starts meeting February 1 and must finish by February 28, and the protest has to be filed ahead of the due date for that year's taxes. If the argument is over classification or taxability, you may take it to the Tax Commissioner under West Virginia Code 11-3-24a, which calls for a ruling by the end of February.

The first $20,000 of a homestead's assessed value is exempt from ad valorem tax under West Virginia Code 11-6B-3. To get it, the owner must be 65 or older, or certified permanently and totally disabled, and must use and occupy the home only as a residence.

Residency counts too: two consecutive calendar years in West Virginia before the tax year. If you receive a similar exemption in another state, you cannot claim this one.

As a seller, you lose little, but the buyer may feel the change. A new owner under 65 does not inherit the exemption, so the bill can go up. Mention that to a financed buyer's agent early so the first tax ticket is no shock.

Before you set a closing date, call the sheriff's tax office for the balance. Current-year tax that is still unpaid can be cleared from your sale proceeds, and a title company will want the number in writing. The table above shows when each half becomes delinquent and starts drawing interest, so you can tell whether your bill has crossed that line.

Pull together a short file before you list: the latest tax ticket, any homestead exemption papers, and records of repairs or water damage. For an inherited house, add the papers showing who the heirs are, since every heir may need to sign.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works in Barbour County
sections.html:
The steps match a normal West Virginia closing, minus the buyer's mortgage. First you describe the house. Next you get a written offer and decide whether to take it. Then an attorney or title company records the deed, pays off liens and settles the tax due.

Cash Home Buyers purchases houses as-is. There are no fees, commissions or closing costs for you, and declining the offer costs nothing.

Sellers in rural counties tend to run into the same few snags:

  • Fewer showings on a listed house, since buyers may have far to drive.
  • Older houses with questions about plumbing, the roof or a septic system.
  • Inherited property with heirs scattered across several states.

A cash offer sidesteps showings and repair negotiations, which is where many listings lose weeks. The one thing it cannot skip is title work, so clear any tax balance and any lien before the closing date.

Plan around the tax calendar. Tax tickets appear in July, and the first half is due in September, so a house that closes in late summer may have a half coming due within weeks. A winter or spring closing falls near the second installment on March 1. In either case, ask the sheriff's tax office what has been paid, and decide with your buyer who covers what.

If you want a quick sale, the order of work looks like this: confirm the tax balance, gather the deed and any lien papers, choose a closing date that suits you, and let the title company order its search. Because no lender is involved in a cash sale, the date is yours to pick, within the time title work takes.

faqs.q: When are Barbour County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Tickets go out on or after July 15. The first installment is due September 1 and the second March 1, and each half turns delinquent on October 1 and April 1.

faqs.q: How do I protest my Barbour County assessment?
faqs.a: Take it to the county commission sitting as the board of equalization and review. The board meets from February 1 until it adjourns by February 28, and you must protest before the taxes are due.

faqs.q: Who gets the West Virginia homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Owners who are 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, and who live in the home may exempt the first $20,000 of assessed value. Apply by December 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Barbour County house with unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The unpaid tax is normally paid out of your proceeds at closing. Get the balance from the sheriff's tax office first.

faqs.q: Does Cash Home Buyers charge fees in Barbour County?
faqs.a: No. We buy as-is, you pay no fees, commissions or closing costs, and you owe nothing if you turn the offer down.
